name: THE SEALED WITH A SWISS BURGER

recipe.history:
Swiss cheese — known properly as Emmental or Emmentaler, named for the Emme valley in the Berne canton of Switzerland — is one of the most recognizable cheeses in the world, largely due to its distinctive large holes or 'eyes.' These holes are not a defect but a signature: they are produced by carbon dioxide gas released by Propionibacterium freudenreichii bacteria during the aging process, which occurs at warm temperatures in special aging rooms maintained around 68–72 degrees Fahrenheit. Emmentaler's production history stretches back to the early 13th century, though the first detailed written records appear in the 15th century. Like Gruyère, it developed in the Alpine cheesemaking tradition where large wheels were a practical necessity — original Emmental wheels weigh between 130 and 220 pounds and were produced in sufficient quantity to sustain families and trading routes through mountain winters. Genuine AOP-protected Emmentaler Switzerland is made from raw milk and aged a minimum of four months, developing a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a springy, elastic texture. The 'Swiss cheese' sold in American supermarkets for most of the 20th century was typically a domestic imitation produced with pasteurized milk and a shorter aging period, milder in flavor but also reliably easy to melt — which is why it became the default cheese of American diner culture.

Swiss cheese's dominance on the American burger is a story of practicality meeting affection. Diner culture in mid-20th century America required cheeses that melted reliably, were mild enough to appeal broadly, and were available at scale — and American-style Swiss delivered on all three counts. The Swiss cheeseburger became a fixture on diner menus from coast to coast, often paired with mushrooms, bacon, or 'secret sauce' combinations that referenced the Swiss cheese's slightly sweet, nutty character without necessarily understanding it. As American cheese culture became more sophisticated, genuine Emmentaler and quality domestic Swiss cheeses with real depth of flavor began replacing the rubbery domestic standby in better burger establishments. The mild sweetness and elegant melt of a quality Swiss on a burger functions as a blank canvas that showcases whatever accompanies it — which is why the Swiss cheeseburger is so often the vehicle for more assertive flavor elements like pickled vegetables, bold sauces, and cured meats.

I ate my first truly good Swiss cheeseburger at a diner counter in Vermont on a ski trip during which I broke my collarbone on the first run and spent the rest of the weekend eating. The diner was the kind of place with a rotating pie case and a cook who didn't speak unless you spoke to him first, and the Swiss cheeseburger was on the menu listed without description as 'Swiss Burger.' What arrived was remarkable: quality beef, cheese melted to the precise point of maximum coverage without pooling, and a set of toppings — thinly sliced ham, a whole grain mustard that someone had made themselves, a pile of watercress — that demonstrated someone in that kitchen had been thinking carefully about Swiss cheese in particular, not just cheese in general. My collarbone healed. That burger lives rent-free in my memory twenty years later.

Swiss cheese is, temperamentally, a gentle cheese — mild in sharpness, generous in melt, cooperative with almost any flavor placed beside it. It achieves its best state on a burger when the patty beneath it is cooked to medium rare, 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, because at that temperature the burger is at its most expressive and the Swiss cheese has a worthy partner. A medium rare patty gives back: its rendered fat enriches the mild cheese, its natural juices blend with the melted Swiss into something more savory and deep than either element alone. Seal the burger at medium rare and the Swiss cheese does what it has always done best — it brings everything together, sealing the flavors of every other ingredient into a coherent, gentle, generous whole. Cook the patty beyond that window and you are sealing nothing. You are only covering your mistake with cheese.
ingredients: For the soft white sandwich buns:
Kosher salt and cracked black pepper
8 oz quality Swiss Emmentaler or domestic Swiss, sliced thin
For the honey whole grain mustard sauce:
For the quick-pickled mustard seed cucumbers:
4 oz quality Black Forest ham or deli ham, thin-sliced
instructions: 1. Make the quick-pickled cucumbers: Combine apple cider vinegar, water, sugar, salt, turmeric, and mustard seeds in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer, stirring until sugar and salt dissolve. Pour over sliced cucumbers in a jar. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate at least 2 hours.
2. Make the sandwich buns: Activate yeast in warm milk with a pinch of sugar, 5–7 minutes until foamy. Combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt in a stand mixer with dough hook.
3. Add yeast mixture, egg, and oil. Mix on low until combined. Add softened butter in pieces. Knead on medium 7–9 minutes until smooth.
4. Cover and let rise 1–1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 6 portions, shape into rounds, and proof 45–60 minutes on parchment-lined sheets.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush buns with egg wash. Bake 15–17 minutes until pale golden. Cool on a rack.

6. Make the honey whole grain mustard sauce: Whisk together both mustards, honey, mayonnaise, white wine vinegar, and salt until smooth. Taste and adjust balance of sweet and sharp. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Form patties: Gently combine ground chuck and sirloin. Divide into 4 portions (~6 oz each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a thumb indent in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and lay Swiss cheese slices over each patty. Cook 2–2.5 minutes more. Pull at 130–132°F. Rest loosely foil-tented 3–4 minutes to reach 133–135°F.
9. While patties rest, warm ham slices briefly in a small pan with butter over medium heat, 1–2 minutes per side.
10. Toast bun halves in butter until golden.

11. Assemble: Spread honey whole grain mustard sauce on both cut bun faces. Place watercress or arugula on the bottom bun. Lay the warmed ham on the greens. Set the rested, Swiss-draped patty on the ham. Top with a layer of pickled mustard seed cucumbers, well-drained. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
